 Flood Warning is in effect Proposed SNAP change could mean more Arizona families lose benefits 
 More than half of Arizona’s SNAP recipients lost benefits year over year, and a new federal proposal could make it harder for more families to qualify. By Amy Cutler Published : Nov. 11, 2026 at 6:45 PM MST | Updated : 10 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google PHOENIX (AZFamily) — A new Trump administration proposal could cut more people from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP, which hundreds of thousands of people in Arizona rely on for food.
 The proposal would stop families who receive other public aid from automatically qualifying for SNAP. State data shows more than half of those receiving SNAP benefits in Arizona were cut from the program following changes put in place in 2025. 
 Families describe reliance on benefits
 The proposal comes as more people are struggling to make ends meet. Food prices are up, and it costs more to fill a gas tank.
 Patricia Martinez, a mother and grandmother, described what SNAP has meant for her family.
 “It is a great help,” Martinez said. “It helps us get our food, so we can use our money elsewhere for utilities, for the rent.”
 Martinez said it keeps getting harder to afford to live in Phoenix.
 “My son works, my daughter-in-law both work, and just along with their incomes we’re barely making it,” she said.
 Arizona cuts followed 2025 work requirements
 States across the country have experienced cuts to SNAP since Republicans enacted new work requirements in July 2025. None were larger than Arizona’s, where more than half of those enrolled lost their benefits year-over-year.
 Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins defended the new proposal.
 “If you are going to be part of a program that depends on taxpayer dollars, we have to make sure that you and your family truly need it,” Rollins said.
 Expert warns of impact on food access
 Hilary Seligman, a doctor and professor at the University of California, San Francisco, studies food access.
 “When SNAP benefits get reduced, or when people lose eligibility for SNAP, there’s less money for food. It means kids are going hungry. It means people are skipping meals,” Seligman said.
 Under this proposal, data shows one in five SNAP enrollees nationally could lose their benefits, and nearly 2 million children could lose free school meals. The federal government argues the change would save nearly $45 billion over five years.
 “There is a small bit of waste, fraud and abuse in the SNAP program. It has been studied very well, and it does exist, and it is very, very small as a percentage of the benefits that are going out,” she said.
 Martinez said free school meals make a difference for the children in her family.
 “They look forward [to] it, going to school in the morning to get their breakfast,” she said.
 Timeline and state response
 The proposed change must undergo a 30-day comment period. It would not take effect until 2029.
 The Arizona Department of Economic Security, the state agency that administers the program, said it is reviewing the policy and could not comment on what it would mean for Arizona.
 Advocates say the proposal might not affect Arizona as much because of the large cuts the state has seen over the last year.
